title_question: How does AI plug into my apps?
also_called: Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Tool Connections
one_liner: MCP is a standard way for AI apps to connect to tools and data (calendar, files, databases) so each connection does not need custom work.

steps.title: The AI client requests capabilities
steps.text: Your AI chat app connects to an MCP server and queries what actions or resources are currently available.

stage_state.description: AI client sending capability inquiry to surrounding tool plugs.

steps.title: An MCP server sits in front of each tool
steps.text: Instead of writing custom code for every calendar or database, a lightweight adapter translates tool actions into standardized messages.

stage_state.description: Standardized adapter box translating proprietary tool formats into universal protocol.

steps.title: You grant explicit permission
steps.text: Before the AI executes an action (such as modifying a calendar event or sending an email), it requests your approval.

stage_state.description: Security prompt requesting user confirmation before action dispatch.

steps.title: Results return into the context window
steps.text: The tool executes the request safely and hands structured results back to the AI to complete your sentence.

stage_state.description: Verified data flowing back through adapter into active conversation.

analogy.text: Think of MCP like USB-C for AI applications. Prior to USB-C, every device required a proprietary charging cable or unique dongle. With a universal port, any compatible peripheral clicks in smoothly.
analogy.breaks: A universal plug design does not make the connected peripheral inherently safe or well-engineered. Careful permission boundaries are still necessary, and data returned from an untrusted tool could contain misleading instructions.

myth.claim: Connecting tools via MCP gives the AI uncontrollable access to delete your files.
myth.reality: MCP architecture requires human-in-the-loop authorization for sensitive actions. You decide which folders or tools are exposed, and can limit connections to read-only access.

seen_in: Claude Desktop using local tools to inspect files and run terminal commands
Cursor and Antigravity IDEs connecting to git repositories and issue trackers
Enterprise AI assistants querying Postgres databases and internal ticketing systems

persona_examples.student: Connecting your notes folder to your study assistant while keeping your personal diary folder disconnected.
persona_examples.teacher: Connecting lesson plan archives while keeping the student grade book in an unlinked, private directory.
persona_examples.entrepreneur: Connecting sales CRM data and calendar availability to automate appointment scheduling with client confirmation.
persona_examples.engineer_office: Granting an AI assistant read-only access to GitHub pull requests and CI/CD logs to analyze failing test runs.

quiz.question: What fundamental problem does the Model Context Protocol (MCP) resolve?
options: It eliminates the need for computer monitors
It replaces hundreds of fragmented, custom tool connectors with one open, universal protocol
It makes computer microchips run ten times cooler
It translates all spoken languages into Latin
quiz.explanation: MCP standardizes how language models communicate with external tools, APIs, and file systems.

quiz.question: Which security habit is recommended when connecting tools to an AI assistant?
options: Grant full administrator write permissions to all drives on your computer
Connect only the specific folders and services required for the immediate task
Share your private passwords with other online chat users
Disable all confirmation prompts to make tools run faster
quiz.explanation: The principle of least privilege ensures the AI only accesses the minimal necessary documents and actions.

quiz.question: Does having a standard connection protocol mean every connected third-party tool is safe?
options: Yes, any tool using a standard protocol is proven 100 percent secure
No, a standard protocol only defines how messages travel; external tools can still contain bugs or return untrusted content
Yes, because protocols replace operating system security
No, protocols only work on mobile phones
quiz.explanation: Protocols standardize communication structure, but application security depends on data validation and user permissions.

explain_back.prompt: Complete this sentence to prove you understand:
explain_back.template: MCP lets an AI connect to external tools using a standard adapter without requiring custom software engineering for every single application.

bullets: MCP uses a client-server architecture with three primitives: Resources (read-only data), Tools (executable actions), and Prompts (predefined templates).
Supported transports include local JSON-RPC over standard input/output (stdio) and remote HTTP with Server-Sent Events (SSE).
Security boundaries mitigate indirect prompt injection vulnerabilities where untrusted tool outputs attempt to override system instructions.
Capability negotiation occurs on initial handshake, allowing clients to advertise supported features and enforce OAuth authorization.

code_panel.title: Minimal MCP Tool Definition
code_panel.code:
# Minimal MCP tool definition (Python SDK)
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("WeatherService")

@mcp.tool()
def get_forecast(city: str) -> str:
    """Retrieve current weather forecast for a specified city."""
    # Safe sandboxed tool execution
    data = fetch_weather_api(city)
    return f"Weather in {city}: {data['summary']}, {data['temp']}°C"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")
